facts.claim: Jason Isbell wrote "If We Were Vampires" as sole songwriter; it was released as the first single from The Nashville Sound.
Isbell wrote the song after his wife Amanda Shires told him to stop watching Hoarders and write, because he was going into the studio the following Monday.
Isbell said he couldn't get through the song the first few times he tried to play it for Shires, and had to leave the room and come back.
The Nashville Sound was produced by Dave Cobb at his RCA Studio A headquarters in Nashville.
Cobb recalled that on the first day of tracking Shires kept saying she couldn't wait for him to hear the 'Vampires' song.
The 400 Unit on the album are Sadler Vaden (guitar), Jimbo Hart (bass), Derry DeBorja (keys), Chad Gamble (drums) and Amanda Shires (fiddle, backing vocals).
Album credits list engineers Matt Ross-Spang and Gena Johnson, mastering by Pete Lyman, and Dave Cobb on acoustic guitar and percussion in addition to producing.
Shires sings harmony vocals on the song, and it has become a live duet showcase for the couple.
The song won Best American Roots Song at the 2018 Grammy Awards; Isbell had also won that category in 2016 with "24 Frames".

Isbell was born Michael Jason Isbell on February 1, 1979 in Green Hill, Alabama; his 2013 breakthrough Southeastern included "Cover Me Up", and Cobb also produced that album and Something More Than Free.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Americana and country singer-songwriter tradition, recorded in Nashville's historic RCA Studio A with producer Dave Cobb, who also produced Isbell's Southeastern and Something More Than Free.

draft:
**If We Were Vampires** spends its whole first stretch saying what love isn't. It isn't the dress, the light on her skin, her hands in the dark, her nails leaving "love's watermark." Each verse sets up a lovely, specific image and then waves it off. Jason Isbell writes the catalog of a devoted husband and then says none of it is the point. The point is that one of them will die first.

That's a strange thing to put at the center of a love song, and Isbell knows it. The vampire verse flips the idea around. If death were a joke, the two of them would stand on the sidewalk smoking, laughing at couples with plans. Then comes the line that holds the whole song: "I wouldn't feel the need to hold your hand." Forever would make love casual. The clock is what makes it urgent, and his reach for her comes from fear as much as tenderness.

The sound stays out of the way. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through steady arpeggios at an unhurried, flowing pace. Isbell's voice is clear with a little rasp at the edges, and a harmony line sits low and close beneath it, the two voices blending until they're hard to pull apart. The room sounds natural and warm, and nothing enters or drops out to dress the moment up. Amanda Shires, Isbell's wife, sings harmony on the song, and it has become a duet showcase for the couple onstage. That fits a song about two people looking at the same ending together.

The writing has its own backstory. Shires told Isbell to stop watching *Hoarders* and write something, since he was heading into the studio that Monday. The first few times he tried to play it for her, he couldn't get through it and had to leave the room. Dave Cobb produced it at RCA Studio A in Nashville for *The Nashville Sound*. He recalled Shires telling him on the first day of tracking that she couldn't wait for him to hear "the 'Vampires' song." It went on to win Best American Roots Song at the 2018 Grammys. It belongs in the plainspoken Americana tradition, where the craft lies in saying something huge in words a person could actually say across a kitchen table.

The last verse is the most honest. He'll work hard to the end of his shift and give her every second he can find, "And hope it isn't me who's left behind." It's a small, selfish wish, because sparing himself the grief means wishing it on her. He says it anyway, and the song doesn't apologize. Then the chorus repeats twice, as if saying it again might make it easier to accept.

The song makes you count the years you might have left with someone, and it makes that counting feel like the most loving thing you could do.
